chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
title: Bothwell's missed Basie job and lost library
summary: Schremp says Bothwell was asked to join Basie but could not tour the South as a white lead alto; his library was lost.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: He told me that he was asked after he left that band--maybe after he left his own band--that he was asked to join the Count on alto.

Not Duke's band, but the Basie band, but he couldn't do it for the reverse reason that they couldn't take that black band through the South with a white lead alto player. They might have a white fourth trumpet player and get by with it, but they couldn't have a white lead alto player, so he lost his Basie gig.
That's weird. How can anybody tell that the white guy is playing lead?

The management took that position. The audience would know he sits in the middle and stands up a lot maybe. It's a highly visible position at any rate. He was the most visible guy on the band for the last few years; it made a virtue of it now currently.
I tell this, I guess, just to have it in the record, because I guess we're never going to do Bothwell. I was looking through the Raeburn charts, he might have taken some with

him, which I guess he did, and his library doesn't exist anymore. He got drunk one night, left it in a hotel in Charleston, South Carolina or some-place and never went back for them. So that's the end of that book.
I find it a little difficult to believe that Basie would have asked him to join. Of course, anything is possible.

He told me that himself when I was putting this thing together. He's not playing now, he hasn't played for years. I told him that he ought to go rent a saxophone and get his chops back in shape. It's pretty funny that I should be telling Bothwell to get his chops back in place.
